mainTopic: Which found produce and coins must be announced: items next to a container, piles, and stacked coins
overview: This amud finishes the משנה's list of found items that must be announced, then works through several of its cases. First the גמרא infers that produce lying in front of a vessel belongs to the finder. It meets a ברייתא that seems to say the opposite and settles the clash in four ways: flax versus produce, whether produce is left in the basket, which way the basket's mouth faces, and whether the basket has a rim. Next it tries to prove from the wording 'piles of produce' that number or location is a סימן, but the wording can be read either way, so there is no proof. רבי יצחק מגדלאה limits the three stacked coins to coins arranged like a tower, and a ברייתא backs him up. רבי חנינא, once his words are restated, requires a graded stack of different-sized coins. רבי יוחנן says even identical coins must be announced, with the count as the סימן, and that is why the משנה needs three coins. Finally רבי ירמיה asks about other coin shapes, and the wood-chip test settles only the ladder. רב אשי then begins a new question that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the list of finds that must be announced
steps.stepSummary: The משנה completes its list of found items that have identifying features, so the finder must announce them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Three coins stacked one on another, bundles of grain in a private area, a homeowner's loaves, wool fleeces taken from a craftsman's house, jugs of wine and jugs of oil: all of these the finder must announce.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes its list of found objects that the finder may not keep. He must announce them so the owner can claim them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each item on the list has something that can identify it, such as a special arrangement, a place, or a person's own style. Because of that, the owner can describe it and get it back, so the finder must announce it.

keyTerms.meaning: to announce a found object publicly so the owner can claim it
an identifying mark or feature (the idea behind this whole list)

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלֹשָׁה מַטְבְּעוֹת זֶה עַל גַּב זֶה,
phrases.english: Three coins, one on top of the other,
bundles of grain in a private area,
and loaves of a homeowner,
and wool fleeces taken from the craftsman's house,
jugs of wine and jugs of oil:
these, he is obligated to announce.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלֹשָׁה מַטְבְּעוֹת זֶה עַל גַּב זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list of items that must be announced, which began earlier on the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Items with identifying features, such as stacked coins, bundles in a private area, homemade loaves, a craftsman's fleeces, and jugs of wine or oil, must be announced.

steps.title: Inference: produce in front of a vessel belongs to the finder
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads closely the משנה's earlier words, 'produce in a vessel, coins in a pouch,' and infers that produce or coins lying in front of the container belong to the finder.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason he must announce is that he found produce inside a vessel or coins inside a pouch. But if he found a vessel with produce in front of it, or a pouch with coins in front of it, these belong to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה's earlier case of produce in a vessel and coins in a pouch. It points out what that wording implies about produce or coins found next to the container.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה requires an announcement only when the produce is inside the vessel. So when the produce is outside it, in front of it, the finder may keep it. We assume the produce did not come from that vessel, and loose produce has no identifying mark.

keyTerms.meaning: the reason (here it introduces a close reading of the exact wording)
but this (it introduces the opposite case that we infer)
these belong to him (the finder keeps them)

steps.confusionAlert: The words 'produce in a vessel, coins in a pouch' are not in this section. They come from the earlier part of the משנה, which the גמרא is now reading closely.

phrases.english: Gemara:
The reason is that he found produce in a vessel
and coins in a pouch.
But a vessel with produce in front of it,
or a pouch with coins in front of it:
these are his.

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דְּמָצָא פֵּירוֹת בִּכְלִי וּמָעוֹת בְּכִיס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא by inferring a new rule from the משנה's wording.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Produce or coins found in front of a container, not inside it, belong to the finder.

steps.title: A ברייתא says the same thing openly
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that a ברייתא states this inference outright, and adds that if the items are partly inside and partly outside, the finder must announce.
steps.simpleTranslation: Our משנה already teaches what the רבנן taught in a ברייתא: if he found a vessel with produce in front of it, or a pouch with coins in front of it, these are his. If some are in the vessel and some on the ground, or some in the pouch and some on the ground, he must announce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the inference it just made from the משנה matches a ברייתא that says it outright.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא confirms that produce fully outside the vessel belongs to the finder. It adds a new case: when some is inside and some is outside, the produce clearly spilled out of that vessel, so it must be announced along with the vessel.

keyTerms.meaning: we have already learned this (our משנה already teaches what the ברייתא says)
the רבנן taught (it introduces a ברייתא)

steps.whyThisMatters: The partly-inside, partly-outside case shows the real test: is there evidence that the produce came out of that container?

phrases.english: We have already learned this,
which the Rabbis taught:
If he found a vessel with produce in front of it,
or a pouch with coins in front of it:
these are his.

phrases.aramaic: מִקְצָתָן בַּכְּלִי וּמִקְצָתָן עַל גַּבֵּי קַרְקַע,
phrases.english: If some are in the vessel and some on the ground,

phrases.aramaic: מִקְצָתָן בַּכִּיס וּמִקְצָתָן עַל גַּבֵּי קַרְקַע –
phrases.english: or some are in the pouch and some on the ground:
he is obligated to announce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the inference of step 2 with a ברייתא that says it outright.
steps.raayaObject: The inference that produce or coins in front of a container belong to the finder.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא (תנו רבנן) that rules this explicitly and adds the partly-inside case.

steps.title: A different ברייתא seems to say the opposite
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא rules that an unmarked item found next to a marked item must be announced. This seems to clash with the rule that produce in front of a vessel belongs to the finder.
steps.simpleTranslation: They contrasted it with this: if he found an item without an identifying mark next to an item with an identifying mark, he must announce. If the owner of the marked item came and took his item, the finder acquires the unmarked item.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the rule from steps 2 and 3 by bringing a ברייתא that seems to rule the opposite way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vessel has a mark and loose produce does not. This ברייתא says that when they are found side by side, both must be announced, as if the unmarked item may belong with the marked one. That contradicts the rule that produce in front of a vessel simply belongs to the finder.

keyTerms.meaning: and they contrasted it (it introduces a source that seems to contradict)
the owner of the marked item
the other one (the finder) acquires it

phrases.english: And they contrasted it:
If he found an item without an identifying mark
next to an item with an identifying mark:
he is obligated to announce.

phrases.aramaic: בָּא בַּעַל סִימָן וְנָטַל אֶת שֶׁלּוֹ –
phrases.english: If the owner of the marked item came and took his,

phrases.aramaic: זָכָה הַלָּה בְּדָבָר שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ סִימָן.
phrases.english: the other one acquires the item without a mark.
phrases.notes: 'The other one' is the finder. The owner did not claim the unmarked item, so the finder keeps it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule established in steps 2 and 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that produce or coins in front of a container belong to the finder.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא requires announcing an unmarked item found next to a marked one. A vessel with produce beside it should be the same case, so the produce should also need announcing.

steps.title: רב זביד: flax and a container versus produce and a basket
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד resolves the contradiction. The ברייתא that requires announcing is about flax next to a container, and the rule that the finder keeps it is about loose produce next to a basket.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said: it is not difficult. This ruling is about a container and flax; that ruling is about a basket and produce.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד answers the challenge by showing that the two rulings deal with different kinds of items.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Flax fibers are tangled together, so if some fall out of a container, all of them come out. Finding the flax completely outside therefore does not prove it was never inside, and it must be announced. Loose produce falls out piece by piece, so if none is left in the basket, it probably never came from there, and the finder keeps it.

keyTerms.meaning: it is not difficult (it introduces a resolution)

steps.whatToRemember: Produce found fully outside a container belongs to the finder, because if it had spilled, some would still be inside. But items that stick together, like flax, can fall out all at once, so they must be announced along with the container.
steps.confusionAlert: Keep the sides straight: the ruling that you must announce is about the container and flax, and the ruling that the finder keeps it is about the basket and produce.

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said: It is not difficult:
this is about a container and flax,
phrases.notes: 'This' is the ברייתא that says you must announce it.

phrases.english: that is about a basket and produce.
phrases.notes: 'That' is the משנה's ruling that the finder keeps it. Loose produce would leave some behind in the basket if it had spilled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each source refers to a different kind of item.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any unmarked item found next to a marked container is treated the same way.
steps.terutzMaskana: It depends on whether the items stick together. Flax beside a container must be announced, while loose produce beside a basket belongs to the finder.

steps.title: רב פפא: Is anything left in the basket?
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says both rulings are about a basket and produce. It depends on whether some produce is still inside the basket.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Both rulings are about a basket and produce, and there is no contradiction. The ruling that you must announce is when some produce is still in the basket. The ruling that the finder keeps it is when nothing is left in the basket.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives his own answer to the contradiction, different from רב זביד's answer. He says both sources are about the same kind of case, a basket with produce near it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב זביד split the cases by type of item: flax versus produce. רב פפא keeps the item the same and looks at the basket instead. If some produce is still inside, the produce outside clearly spilled from it, so the finder must announce. If the basket is empty, we cannot tell that the produce came from it, so the finder keeps it.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
Both this and that are about a basket and produce,
phrases.notes: 'This and that' are the two sources from step 4: the ברייתא that says announce, and the משנה's rule that the finder keeps it.

phrases.english: and it is not difficult:
this is where something remained in it,
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא. Since some produce is still in the basket, it is clear the rest spilled out of it.

phrases.english: that is where nothing remained in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא אָמַר: הָא וְהָא בְּצַנָּא וּפֵירֵי, וְלָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the same contradiction that רב זביד resolved
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: produce remaining inside the basket versus an empty basket
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two sources seem to give opposite rulings about the same kind of situation.
steps.terutzMaskana: If produce remains in the basket, announce. If the basket is empty, the finder keeps it.

steps.title: Another answer: Which way the basket's mouth faces
steps.stepSummary: Even when the basket is empty, it depends on whether the basket's opening faces the produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: Both rulings are about a basket with nothing left in it, and there is no contradiction. The ruling that you must announce is when the basket's mouth faces the produce. The ruling that the finder keeps it is when the mouth does not face the produce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another way to settle the contradiction. This time both cases are about an empty basket.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer allows that the ברייתא might also be about an empty basket. If the basket's opening points toward the produce, it looks like the produce spilled out of it, so it must be announced. If the opening points away, there is no sign of a connection, so the finder keeps it.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say: introduces another possible answer

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:

phrases.aramaic: הָא וְהָא דְּלָא אִשְׁתְּיַיר בַּהּ מִידֵּי,
phrases.english: both this and that are where nothing remained in it,
and it is not difficult:
this is where its mouth is turned toward the produce,
phrases.notes: Literally 'its face.' He means the opening of the basket.

phrases.aramaic: הָא דְּלָא מְהַדְּרִי אַפֵּיהּ לְגַבֵּי פֵּירֵי.
phrases.english: that is where its mouth is not turned toward the produce.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא דְּלָא אִשְׁתְּיַיר בַּהּ מִידֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows to an empty basket and offers a new way to split the cases
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by the direction of the basket's opening
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An empty basket might mean the finder always keeps the produce.
steps.terutzMaskana: Opening facing the produce means announce. Opening facing away means the finder keeps it.

steps.title: Another answer: Whether the basket has a rim
steps.stepSummary: Even when the empty basket's mouth faces the produce, it depends on whether the basket has a rim.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: Both rulings are about a basket whose mouth faces the produce, and there is no contradiction. One ruling is when the basket has a rim, and the other is when the basket has no rim.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third way to settle the contradiction. This time both cases are about an empty basket that faces the produce.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the basket has a rim and the produce had spilled from it, the rim would have held back a little produce. Since the basket is completely empty, the produce probably did not come from it, so the finder keeps it. If there is no rim, everything could have slid out, so the finder must announce.

keyTerms.meaning: It has / it does not have

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the order here. The first 'הא' (has a rim) is the case where the finder KEEPS the produce, and the second 'הא' (no rim) is where he must announce. This is the reverse of the order in the earlier answers.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:

phrases.aramaic: הָא וְהָא דִּמְהַדְּרִי אַפֵּיהּ לְגַבֵּי פֵּירֵי,
phrases.english: both this and that are where its mouth is turned toward the produce,
and it is not difficult:
this is where the basket has a rim,
phrases.notes: This is the משנה's case, where the finder keeps it. A rim would have trapped some produce if it had spilled from this basket.

phrases.english: that is where the basket has no rim.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: הָא וְהָא דִּמְהַדְּרִי אַפֵּיהּ לְגַבֵּי פֵּירֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows further to an empty basket facing the produce and splits the cases by whether it has a rim
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by the shape of the basket (rim or no rim)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A basket facing the produce might always mean the produce must be announced.
steps.terutzMaskana: With a rim, an empty basket shows the produce did not come from it, so the finder keeps it. Without a rim, the finder must announce.
steps.whatToRemember: Three answers follow רב זביד's answer, and each looks at one more detail: whether produce is left inside, which way the opening faces, and whether there is a rim. Each detail asks one question: does it look like this produce fell out of this basket?

steps.title: Trying to prove that the number of piles is a סימן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words 'piles of produce' and tries to learn that the number of piles counts as a סימן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'Piles of produce and piles of coins' must be announced. Learn from this that the number of piles is an identifying sign.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line in the משנה. It tries to draw a proof from its plural wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה uses the plural 'piles.' The גמרא suggests this means the owner can claim them by saying how many piles there were. That would show that a number counts as a סימן.

keyTerms.meaning: An identifying sign used to claim a lost item

phrases.english: Piles of produce and piles of coins.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from the משנה's list of found items that must be announced.

phrases.english: Learn from it that a number is an identifying sign.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic based on a different phrase in the משנה
steps.raayaObject: That a number counts as a סימן
steps.raayaSupportSource: The plural wording 'צבורי פירות' in the משנה

steps.title: Maybe the משנה says 'a pile' in the singular
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof by suggesting the משנה might read 'a pile of produce' in the singular.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps read the משנה as saying 'a pile of produce.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from the plural wording. It says the wording might actually be singular.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה says 'a pile' in the singular, there is no number to count. So the proof that a number is a סימן falls away.

phrases.english: Read: 'A pile of produce.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 9
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that a number is a סימן
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof relies on the plural wording, but the wording might be singular.

steps.title: Then prove that location is a סימן
steps.stepSummary: Building on the singular reading, the גמרא tries to prove that the location of the item counts as a סימן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then learn from this that location is an identifying sign.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes the singular reading and draws a new proof from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A single pile has no number to identify it. So if it must be announced, the owner must claim it by saying where it was. That would show that location counts as a סימן.

phrases.english: Learn from it that location is an identifying sign.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds a new proof on the singular reading from step 10
steps.raayaObject: That location counts as a סימן

steps.title: Maybe the משנה really says 'piles' after all
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects this proof too, because the משנה might really read 'piles' in the plural. So no proof works either way.
steps.simpleTranslation: Perhaps read the משנה as saying 'piles of produce.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back again by returning to the plural reading. This cancels the proof about location.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the משנה says 'piles,' the owner might identify them by their number, not their location. Since we cannot be sure whether the wording is singular or plural, the משנה cannot prove that either number or location is a סימן.
steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא goes back and forth between 'pile' and 'piles' to show that the משנה's wording cannot decide the question. It does not prove that number is a סימן, and it does not prove that location is a סימן.

phrases.english: Read: 'Piles of produce.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from step 11 by returning to the plural reading
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that location is a סימן
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof relies on the singular reading, but the plural reading is just as possible.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The משנה's wording cannot prove whether number or location is a סימן.

steps.title: Coins must be stacked like a tower
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of three stacked coins, and רבי יצחק מגדלאה limits it to coins arranged like towers.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says three coins one on top of another must be announced. רבי יצחק מגדלאה says this is only when they are arranged like towers.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: the משנה's case of three stacked coins. רבי יצחק מגדלאה adds a condition to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה just says 'three coins one on top of another.' רבי יצחק מגדלאה makes this narrower: the coins must form a neat tower. Only then is the stacking itself a סימן that the owner can identify.

keyTerms.meaning: רבי יצחק from the town of מגדל

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלֹשָׁה מַטְבְּעוֹת זֶה עַל גַּב זֶה.
phrases.english: Three coins, one on top of another.
phrases.notes: These are the משנה's words, from its list of finds you must announce.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak from Migdal said:
And this is only when they are arranged like towers.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק מַגְדְּלָאָה: וְהוּא שֶׁעֲשׂוּיִין כְּמִגְדָּלִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case from the משנה after the discussion of piles of produce ended without a proof.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three stacked coins need to be announced only when they are arranged like towers.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports the tower rule
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that scattered coins belong to the finder, while coins arranged like towers must be announced.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא also teaches this: scattered coins belong to the finder. Coins arranged like towers must be announced, and 'towers' means three coins one on top of another.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that says the same thing as רבי יצחק מגדלאה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא separates two cases. Scattered coins have no סימן, so they belong to the finder. Tower-stacked coins must be announced. It also defines a 'tower' as three coins one on top of another, which ties it directly to the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: a ברייתא also teaches this, which is support

phrases.english: It is also taught like this:

phrases.aramaic: מָצָא מָעוֹת מְפוּזָּרוֹת – הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁלּוֹ,
phrases.english: If he found scattered coins, these belong to him;
if they are arranged like towers, he must announce.
And which are 'arranged like towers'?

phrases.aramaic: שְׁלֹשָׁה מַטְבְּעִין זֶה עַל גַּב זֶה.
phrases.english: Three coins, one on top of another.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי יצחק מגדלאה's condition.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יצחק מגדלאה's rule that the coins must be arranged like towers
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא contrasting scattered coins with tower-stacked coins

steps.title: The ברייתא seems to contradict itself
steps.stepSummary: Each half of the ברייתא implies the opposite ruling about coins that only partly overlap.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא itself is difficult. The first part says scattered coins are his, which implies partly overlapping coins must be announced. The second part says tower coins must be announced, which implies partly overlapping coins are his.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a contradiction inside the ברייתא it just quoted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a middle case: coins that partly overlap. They are not fully scattered, and they are not a neat tower. The first part of the ברייתא suggests only 'scattered' coins are the finder's. The second part suggests only 'tower' coins must be announced. So the middle case gets opposite rulings.

keyTerms.meaning: this source itself is difficult, meaning it contradicts itself

steps.confusionAlert: The contradiction comes only from what each half implies, not from what it says outright. Each half has an unstated 'but not this other case,' and those two hidden implications clash over the partly-overlapping coins.

phrases.english: This itself is difficult:

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרַתְּ מָצָא מָעוֹת מְפוּזָּרוֹת הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁלּוֹ,
phrases.english: You said: if he found scattered coins, these are his;
so if they partly overlap, he must announce!
Now say the last part:
if arranged like towers, he must announce;

phrases.aramaic: הָא מְשַׁלְחֲפִי שַׁלְחוֹפֵי הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁלּוֹ!
phrases.english: so if they partly overlap, these are his!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the inner consistency of the ברייתא brought as support.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא of scattered coins versus tower coins
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first half implies partly overlapping coins must be announced. The second half implies they belong to the finder.

steps.title: Anything not a tower counts as scattered
steps.stepSummary: The תנא calls every arrangement that is not a neat tower 'scattered,' so partly overlapping coins belong to the finder.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תנא calls anything that is not arranged like towers 'scattered.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by explaining how the ברייתא uses the word 'scattered.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second half of the ברייתא is the exact one. Only a neat tower must be announced. The word 'scattered' in the first half is broad and includes partly overlapping coins, so those belong to the finder.

phrases.english: The teacher, anything not arranged like towers,
calls them 'scattered.'

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא כֹּל שֶׁאֵין עֲשׂוּיִין כְּמִגְדָּלִין מְפוּזָּרוֹת קָרֵי לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction in step 15.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Scattered' means only fully spread-out coins, which leaves partly overlapping coins in doubt.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Scattered' covers everything that is not a neat tower, so partly overlapping coins belong to the finder.
steps.whatToRemember: Only a true tower of coins must be announced. Anything less, even partly overlapping coins, counts as 'scattered' and belongs to the finder.

steps.title: רבי חנינא: only coins of three kings
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא limits the rule of stacked coins to coins minted by three different kings.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said: this was taught only about coins of three kings. Coins of one king do not need to be announced.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא adds another condition to the משנה's case of three stacked coins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taken at face value, רבי חנינא says the coins must come from three different kings. If all of them come from one king, the finder keeps them. The next step will question what case he could mean.

keyTerms.meaning: an אמורא who adds a condition here
kings, meaning coins minted by different rulers

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁל שְׁלֹשָׁה מְלָכִים,
phrases.english: They taught this only about coins of three kings,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל שֶׁל מֶלֶךְ אֶחָד אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב לְהַכְרִיז.
phrases.english: but with coins of one king, he does not have to announce.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁל שְׁלֹשָׁה מְלָכִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a new condition to the same משנה case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Stacked coins must be announced only if they come from three different kings.

steps.title: What case could רבי חנינא mean?
steps.stepSummary: Whether the coins are a tower or not, the number of kings should not matter.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If they are arranged like towers, even coins of one king should be announced. If they are not arranged like towers, even coins of three kings should not be announced!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי חנינא by showing that his condition does not seem to matter in either possible case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule depends on whether the coins form a tower. If they do, that is already enough to require an announcement, whoever minted them. If they don't, they are 'scattered' and belong to the finder, even from three kings. So which kings minted the coins seems to make no difference.

keyTerms.meaning: if this... and if that, setting out two options

phrases.english: What is the case?
If they are arranged like towers,
then even coins of one king also need announcing;
and if they are not arranged like towers,

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ שֶׁל שְׁלֹשָׁה מְלָכִים נָמֵי לָא!
phrases.english: then even coins of three kings should not need it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי חנינא's condition.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חנינא's condition about three kings
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Whether the coins form a tower already decides the ruling, so the number of kings changes nothing.

steps.title: רבי חנינא restated: one king's coins that look like three kings'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא restates רבי חנינא: the rule applies to one king's coins that resemble three kings' coins, but not to plain coins of one king.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if it was said, this is how it was said: they taught this only about coins of one king that are like coins of three kings. But plain coins of one king do not need to be announced.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by changing how רבי חנינא's words are reported.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Three kings' was not meant literally. It describes coins that look different from one another, like coins from three different kings, even if one king minted them all. The next lines explain that this means coins of different sizes.

keyTerms.meaning: rather, if it was said, this is how it was said, which rewords an אמורא's statement

phrases.english: Rather, if it was said, this is how it was said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא שֶׁל מֶלֶךְ אֶחָד
phrases.english: They taught this only about coins of one king
that are like coins of three kings,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל שֶׁל מֶלֶךְ אֶחָד אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב לְהַכְרִיז.
phrases.english: but with coins of one king, he does not have to announce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 18 by rewording רבי חנינא's statement.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי חנינא literally meant coins minted by three different kings.
steps.terutzMaskana: He meant one king's coins that differ from each other like three kings' coins would.

steps.title: What does a tower look like in this case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what exactly the tower case is under this new reading.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the case of coins arranged like towers?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question to set up its explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now that the case is 'one king's coins that look like three kings',' the גמרא wants to describe exactly how such coins form a tower.

phrases.english: And what is the case of coins arranged like towers?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for details of the restated teaching.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How a tower of different-looking coins is arranged

steps.title: Biggest on the bottom, smallest on top
steps.stepSummary: A stack going from wide to small shows someone placed it on purpose. Same-size coins may have fallen together by chance.
steps.simpleTranslation: The widest coin is on the bottom, the middle-sized one is on it, and the smallest is on the middle one. We say someone put them there. But coins of one king are all the same size, so even if they lie on each other, they belong to the finder. We can say it just happened that they fell together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question and explains why only a stack of graded sizes counts as a tower that must be announced.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Coins arranged from widest to smallest are clearly set down by a person, so the arrangement is a real סימן. Same-size coins in a pile could easily have landed that way by accident, so the stacking shows nothing and the finder keeps them.

keyTerms.meaning: someone placed them there on purpose

steps.whatToRemember: A stack of three coins counts as a tower only when it is graded: widest on the bottom, middle in the middle, smallest on top. This proves someone set them down. Same-size coins in a pile could have fallen together by chance, so they belong to the finder.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the general idea behind a סימן based on how an item is arranged. The arrangement counts only if it could not easily have happened by accident.

phrases.english: The widest is on the bottom,
and the middle-sized one is on it,
and the small one is on the middle one.
For we say: someone placed them there.
But with coins of one king,
where all of them are the same as each other,
even though they lie on top of each other,
these belong to him (the finder),
for I can say: it just happened by chance,
and they fell together.

steps.triggerLanguage: רְוִיחָא תַּתָּאָה וּמְצִיעָא עִילָּוֵיהּ וְזוּטָא עִילָּוֵיהּ מְצִיעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 20 and finishes explaining רבי חנינא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A tower is graded coins, widest on the bottom and smallest on top. That shows intentional placement, unlike same-size coins that could have fallen together by chance.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Only a graded stack of different-sized coins must be announced. Same-size stacked coins belong to the finder.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: Even one king's coins must be announced
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules that even coins minted by a single king must be announced when found in a tower.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: Even if the coins are from one king, he must also announce them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן disagrees with רבי חנינא. He says that a tower of coins from one king must also be announced.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנינא limited the rule to coins that look like they come from three kings. רבי יוחנן says the king does not matter, because the tower arrangement itself shows the coins were placed on purpose. This raises a question: what סימן will the owner give?

keyTerms.meaning: Announces publicly that he found something
One king (coins minted by a single ruler)

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
Even coins of one king,
he must also announce.
phrases.notes: He is arguing with רבי חנינא from a few lines earlier, who said plain same-size coins of one king belong to the finder.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents an opposing view to רבי חנינא's limitation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even a tower of coins from one king must be announced.

steps.title: What sign does the owner give?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the finder announces, meaning what identifying sign the owner can offer.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does he announce?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question. If all the coins look alike, how will the real owner prove they are his?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Announcing only makes sense if the owner can give a סימן. Plain coins from one king seem to have no special sign, so the גמרא asks what that sign would be.

phrases.english: What does he announce?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how רבי יוחנן's ruling works in practice.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What identifying sign is available for identical coins of one king.

steps.title: The number of coins is the sign
steps.stepSummary: The owner identifies the coins by saying how many there were.
steps.simpleTranslation: The number.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the owner proves ownership by saying how many coins he lost.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The coins look alike, but the count is a real סימן. The finder announces that he found coins, and the owner must state the correct number.

phrases.english: The number.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of what sign is used.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The owner states the number of coins.

steps.title: Why does the משנה say three coins?
steps.stepSummary: If the count is the sign, then two coins should be enough, so why does the משנה mention three?
steps.simpleTranslation: Why specifically three? Even two would also work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer. If the number is the sign, the משנה could have spoken about two coins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's case involves three coins. If counting works as a sign, two coins could also be counted, so the number three seems unnecessary.

phrases.english: Why specifically three?
Even two should also work.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the count answer using the wording of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the number of coins is the sign.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the count works as a sign, the משנה's choice of three coins seems pointless, since two could be counted too.

steps.title: רבינא: The word 'coins' already means two
steps.stepSummary: רבינא explains that the finder announces 'coins' in the plural, so saying 'two' gives no real sign.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: He announces 'coins.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers the challenge. The finder announces that he found 'coins,' which already tells everyone there were at least two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plural word means at least two. So an owner who says 'two' is only repeating what the announcement already revealed. Only three or more is a real סימן, and that is why the משנה says three.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who gives the answer here

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוחנן, even identical coins in a tower are announced, and the count is the sign. It must be at least three, because the plural 'coins' already means two.

phrases.english: Ravina said:
He announces 'coins.'
phrases.notes: Saying 'coins' in the plural already tells everyone there were at least two, so 'two' proves nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge about the number three.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why two is not a usable sign
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Two coins could be identified by their count.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two is already known from the plural announcement, so the smallest real sign is three.

steps.title: רבי ירמיה asks about four coin arrangements
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks what the law is for coins found in a circle, in a line, in a triangle, or like a ladder.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה asked: If they are like a bracelet, what is the law? Like a row? Like a triangle? Like a ladder?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה opens a new topic. He asks whether other shapes, not only a tower, show that someone arranged the coins on purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A tower requires announcing because it shows the coins were placed deliberately. רבי ירמיה asks about four other shapes: a circle, a straight line, a triangle, and a ladder where each coin partly overlaps the next. The question is whether any of these also count as deliberate placement.

keyTerms.meaning: Asks, raises a question he cannot yet answer
Ladder, coins partly overlapping each other

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya asked:
Like a bracelet, what is the law?
phrases.notes: Coins laid out in a circle.

phrases.english: Like a row, what is the law?
Like a tripod, what is the law?
Like a ladder, what is the law?
phrases.notes: Each coin sits partly on the one below it and sticks out, like steps.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the tower case to other arrangements.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a circle, line, triangle, or ladder arrangement counts as deliberate and requires announcing.

steps.title: The wood-chip test settles the ladder case
steps.stepSummary: Using רבה בר אבוה's rule, the גמרא settles one question: if a wood chip slipped between the coins could lift them all together, the finder must announce.
steps.simpleTranslation: Settle one of them from this, as רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: Any case where, if he slips a wood chip between them, he can lift them all at once, he must announce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles one of רבי ירמיה's questions using an earlier rule. If one wood chip can lift all the coins together, they must be announced.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is whether the coins are connected enough to be lifted as a single unit. Coins in a ladder overlap, so a chip slipped between them lifts them all, which means the finder announces. The rule only says when the finder must announce. It does not say that coins failing the test belong to the finder, so the circle, line and triangle stay unsettled.
steps.whatToRemember: A ladder arrangement must be announced, because a wood chip slipped between the coins can lift them all at once.

phrases.english: Settle one of them from this,
phrases.notes: Only one of the four questions gets answered here: the ladder.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ:
phrases.english: as Rav Naḥman said in the name of Rabba bar Avuh:

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל שֶׁאִילּוּ מַכְנִיס לָהֶ[ן] קֵיסָם בֵּינֵיהֶן
phrases.english: any case where, if he slips a wood chip between them,
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is the corrected spelling; some versions don't have it.

phrases.english: and lifts them all at once,
he must announce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers part of רבי ירמיה's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Coins in a ladder must be announced, because a chip can lift them together.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב נחמן in the name of רבה בר אבוה

steps.title: רב אשי begins a new question
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי opens a new question, which continues in the next lines.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי asked:
steps.whatsHappening: This line is a setup. רב אשי is about to ask his own question, and its content comes right after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'בעי רב אשי' introduce a new question on the same topic of found objects and signs. The question itself appears in the text that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: A later אמורא who raises the next question

phrases.english: Rav Ashi asked:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a new question after רבי ירמיה's questions.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Not yet stated. The question follows in the next lines.
